## Proof

Let $F$ be a distribution function, so $F$ is non-decreasing, right-continuous, with $\lim_{x\to-\infty}F(x)=0$ and $\lim_{x\to+\infty}F(x)=1$. Let $\mu$ be the probability measure on $\mathbb{R}$ associated to $F$, i.e. $F(x)=\mu((-\infty,x])$.

**Claim.** For every $a\in\mathbb{R}$,
$$\int_{\mathbb{R}}\bigl(F(x+a)-F(x)\bigr)\,dx \;=\; a.$$

**Case 1: $a\ge 0$.** Since $F$ is non-decreasing, $F(x+a)-F(x)\ge 0$, and
$$F(x+a)-F(x)=\mu\bigl((x,x+a]\bigr)=\int_{\mathbb{R}}\mathbf{1}_{(x,x+a]}(y)\,d\mu(y).$$
By Tonelli's theorem (all integrands are non-negative),
$$\int_{\mathbb{R}}\bigl(F(x+a)-F(x)\bigr)\,dx=\int_{\mathbb{R}}\int_{\mathbb{R}}\mathbf{1}_{(x,x+a]}(y)\,dx\,d\mu(y).$$
Now $\mathbf{1}_{(x,x+a]}(y)=1$ iff $x<y\le x+a$, i.e. $y-a\le x<y$. Hence
$$\int_{\mathbb{R}}\mathbf{1}_{(x,x+a]}(y)\,dx=\int_{y-a}^{y}dx=a.$$
Therefore
$$\int_{\mathbb{R}}\bigl(F(x+a)-F(x)\bigr)\,dx=\int_{\mathbb{R}}a\,d\mu(y)=a\cdot\mu(\mathbb{R})=a\cdot 1=a.$$

**Case 2: $a<0$.** Set $b=-a>0$. Then $F(x+a)-F(x)=F(x-b)-F(x)\le 0$, so $G(x):=F(x)-F(x+a)=F(x)-F(x-b)\ge 0$. Applying the computation of Case 1 with $b$ in place of $a$,
$$\int_{\mathbb{R}}\bigl(F(x)-F(x-b)\bigr)\,dx=b=-a.$$
Hence
$$\int_{\mathbb{R}}\bigl(F(x+a)-F(x)\bigr)\,dx=-\int_{\mathbb{R}}G(x)\,dx=-b=a.$$

**Well-definedness.** The integrand vanishes at both ends: as $x\to+\infty$, $F(x+a)-F(x)\to 1-1=0$; as $x\to-\infty$, $F(x+a)-F(x)\to 0-0=0$. The Tonelli/Fubini computation above shows the integral is finite, so it is well-defined (no $\pm\infty$ ambiguity).

Combining both cases, for every $a\in\mathbb{R}$,
$$\boxed{\int_{\mathbb{R}}\bigl(F(x+a)-F(x)\bigr)\,dx=a.}$$

$$\int_{\mathbb{R}}\bigl(F(x+a)-F(x)\bigr)\,dx=\int_{\mathbb{R}}\int_{\mathbb{R}}\mathbf{1}_{(x,x+a]}(y)\,dx\,d\mu(y).$$
Now $\mathbf{1}_{(x,x+a]}(y)=1$ iff $x<y\le x+a$, i.e. $y-a\le x<y$. Hence
$$\int_{\mathbb{R}}\mathbf{1}_{(x,x+a]}(y)\,dx=\int_{y-a}^{y}dx=a.$$
Therefore
$$\int_{\mathbb{R}}\bigl(F(x+a)-F(x)\bigr)\,dx=\int_{\mathbb{R}}a\,d\mu(y)=a\cdot\mu(\mathbb{R})=a\cdot 1=a.$$

**Case 2: $a<0$.** Set $b=-a>0$. Then $F(x+a)-F(x)=F(x-b)-F(x)\le 0$, so $G(x):=F(x)-F(x+a)=F(x)-F(x-b)\ge 0$. Applying the computation of Case 1 with $b$ in place of $a$,
$$\int_{\mathbb{R}}\bigl(F(x)-F(x-b)\bigr)\,dx=b=-a.$$
Hence
$$\int_{\mathbb{R}}\bigl(F(x+a)-F(x)\bigr)\,dx=-\int_{\mathbb{R}}G(x)\,dx=-b=a.$$

**Well-definedness.** The integrand vanishes at both ends: as $x\to+\infty$, $F(x+a)-F(x)\to 1-1=0$; as $x\to-\infty$, $F(x+a)-F(x)\to 0-0=0$. The Tonelli/Fubini computation above shows the integral is finite, so it is well-defined (no $\pm\infty$ ambiguity).
